cat.Islamique (XVIIe s. sur fondation mediev: Islamic (17th century, built on medieval foundations)
cat.Antiquite (Tacapae) a nos jours: From antiquity (Tacapae) to the present day
cat.Ottomane (XVIe s., sur fondations anteri: Ottoman (16th century, built on earlier foundations)
cat.Romain / Byzantin, reconstruit au XVIe s: Roman / Byzantine, rebuilt in the 16th century

carthage.d: A city founded by the Phoenicians, capital of the Punic empire and later a major Roman city in Africa. An extensive archaeological site (the Byrsa hills, harbours, thermal baths) listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
carthage.a: Byrsa Hill and its museum; the circular and rectangular Punic harbours; the Antonine Baths by the sea; the Tophet of Salammbô and the Roman villas at the Odeon.
carthage.c: Allow half a day and buy the combined ticket valid for all areas, which are spread over several kilometres.
carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

byrsa.d: A hill that formed the acropolis of Punic Carthage, the site of the citadel, and later the monumental centre of Roman Carthage. Home to the National Museum of Carthage.
byrsa.a: The excavated Punic quarter on the hillside; the National Museum of Carthage; the panoramic view of the ancient harbours and the Gulf of Tunis.
byrsa.c: Head up in the late morning to catch the light over the bay, then carry on to the neighbouring Saint-Louis Cathedral.
byrsa.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

portspuniquesdecarthage.d: The two ancient harbours of Carthage: a rectangular merchant harbour and a circular military harbour (the Admiralty Harbour). Remains still visible in the present-day landscape.
portspuniquesdecarthage.a: the circular Admiralty islet and the water area of the military harbour; the rectangular merchant harbour; the scale model at the small Antiquarium museum.
portspuniquesdecarthage.c: A quick site to visit, best combined with the nearby Tophet.
portspuniquesdecarthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

tophetdecarthage.d: The open-air sanctuary of Punic Carthage (the Tophet of Salammbo), where funerary urns and votive stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit were placed.
tophetdecarthage.a: Hundreds of votive stelae to Baal Hammon and Tanit; funerary urns lined up in the open-air enclosure.
tophetdecarthage.c: A short visit; arrive early before the heat sets in and combine it with a visit to the adjacent Punic ports.
tophetdecarthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

thermesdantonin.d: Vast public baths built in Carthage during the reign of Antoninus Pius, on the seafront. Among the largest baths in the Roman world.
thermesdantonin.a: The imposing substructures by the sea (the vaulted service level that supported the halls), the tall column that gives a sense of the building’s dizzying scale (originally over 30 metres high), the frigidarium and the pools, and the view over the Gulf of Tunis.
thermesdantonin.c: Combine a visit with the other sites in Carthage (Byrsa and its museum, Roman villas) on the same ticket; come in the morning to enjoy the light and the cool sea air – allow around 45 minutes.
thermesdantonin.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

amphitheatredecarthage.d: The amphitheatre of Roman Carthage, largely levelled, is traditionally associated with the martyrdom of Saints Perpetua and Felicity.
amphitheatredecarthage.a: The levelled arena and the commemorative cross marking the martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity; the remains of the stands.
amphitheatredecarthage.c: A modest site, best included as part of a wider tour of the ruins of Carthage.
amphitheatredecarthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

citernesdelamalga.d: A complex of large Roman cisterns which stored the water supplied to Carthage by the Zaghouan aqueduct.
citernesdelamalga.a: The long series of parallel vaulted galleries of the immense Roman reservoir that received water from the Zaghouan aqueduct, parts of which have been reused for housing.
citernesdelamalga.c: A quiet, off-the-beaten-track site; well worth a visit alongside the nearby Byrsa.

cathedralesaintlouisdecarthage.d: A former Catholic cathedral built in the late 19th century on Byrsa Hill. Now deconsecrated, it serves as a cultural centre (Acropolium).
cathedralesaintlouisdecarthage.a: The Neo-Byzantine and Moorish façade; the interior, converted into a cultural centre (the Acropolium); the viewpoint on Byrsa Hill.
cathedralesaintlouisdecarthage.c: Make the most of the terrace for the view, just after visiting the Carthage Museum.

utiqueutica.d: An ancient Phoenician city, one of the oldest in North Africa, which later became an important Roman city. Remains of houses with mosaics and necropolises. Today it lies approximately 10 km from the sea (due to silting up of the Medjerda delta).
utiqueutica.a: The House of the Waterfall and its mosaics still in situ; the remains of the thermal baths; the small museum displaying Punic sarcophagi and pottery.
utiqueutica.c: A quiet, off-the-beaten-track site; combine your visit with a stop at the Utica Museum on site.
utiqueutica.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

kerkouane.d: A Punic city abandoned around the 3rd century BC and never rebuilt, a rare example of Phoenician-Punic urban planning. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
kerkouane.a: The complete plan of the Punic city with streets and houses; the pink-coloured baths of the private bathing quarters; the small museum and the rock-cut necropolis.
kerkouane.c: The only purely Punic city to have been preserved; best visited in conjunction with the Cap Bon coast and Kelibia.
kerkouane.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season; please check on site.

necropoledekerkouane.d: Rock-cut necropolis associated with the Punic city of Kerkouane, featuring tombs carved into the rock.
necropoledekerkouane.a: Punic tombs carved into the rock, serving as a burial complement to the neighbouring city of Kerkouane.
necropoledekerkouane.c: Well worth a visit whilst you’re at the Kerkouane site, to which it is linked.

douggathugga.d: An ancient city of Numidian and later Roman origin, it is one of the best-preserved ancient sites in North Africa (capitol, theatre, temples, Libyco-Punic mausoleum). Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
douggathugga.a: the Capitol with its Corinthian columns; the theatre set against the hillside; the Libyco-Punic mausoleum; the Place des Vents and the latrines with twelve seats.
douggathugga.c: Extensive ruins on a slope: walking shoes and at least two hours; magnificent in the low morning sun.
douggathugga.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

capitolededougga.d: The Capitol of Thugga, dedicated to the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter, Juno, Minerva), was built in the 2nd century. Its colonnaded façade is one of the site’s most iconic monuments.
capitolededougga.a: The tall façade with six Corinthian columns and its sculpted pediment; the podium overlooking the forum.
capitolededougga.c: An iconic monument of the site; best photographed early in the day to avoid backlighting.
capitolededougga.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary depending on the season, so please check on site.

theatrededougga.d: The Roman Theatre of Thugga, built in the 2nd century, set against the hillside and well-preserved, is still used for performances.
theatrededougga.a: The well-preserved tiers of seating for around 3,500 spectators; the stage and the view over the plain of the Khalled wadi.
theatrededougga.c: Sit at the top of the tiers to enjoy the panoramic view; still used in summer for performances.
theatrededougga.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary depending on the season, so please check on site.

amphitheatredeljemthysdrus.d: The grand Roman amphitheatre of ancient Thysdrus, dating from the 3rd century, is one of the best-preserved in the world. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
amphitheatredeljemthysdrus.a: The superimposed arcades of the façade; the arena and the underground passages through which animals and gladiators passed; the tiers of seating that you can climb.
amphitheatredeljemthysdrus.c: Climb to the upper levels for the view; combine your visit with the El Jem Museum and its mosaics.
amphitheatredeljemthysdrus.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

sbeitlasufetula.d: An ancient Roman and Byzantine city notable for its forum and its three adjoining Capitoline temples, as well as its Christian basilicas.
sbeitlasufetula.a: The Sufetula forum, with its paved floor, opens onto three adjoining Capitoline temples dedicated to the Triad, the Arch of Antoninus Pius and several Christian basilicas with baptisteries.
sbeitlasufetula.c: Allow 2 to 3 hours for your visit and make the most of the low-angle light in the morning or late afternoon to photograph the Capitoline temples.
sbeitlasufetula.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

capitoledesbeitla.d: An exceptional complex of three distinct Capitoline temples dedicated to the triad, opening onto the Forum of Sufetula.
capitoledesbeitla.a: The three distinct and well-preserved Capitoline temples, aligned behind the arch and the forum, represent a rare example of a triad comprising separate buildings.
capitoledesbeitla.c: Best combined with the wider Sufetula site in the immediate vicinity; just a few minutes are needed to see this highlight.
capitoledesbeitla.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so please check on site.

bullaregia.d: A Roman town known for its villas with underground floors designed to provide relief from the heat, adorned with mosaics still in situ (House of the Hunt, House of Amphitrite).
bullaregia.a: The villas with underground levels (House of the Hunt, House of Amphitrite) featuring mosaics in situ; the theatre and the baths of Julia Memmia.
bullaregia.c: Descend into the underground houses, which remain cool even in the height of summer; mosaics can be seen in situ.
bullaregia.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season; please check on site.

thuburbomajus.d: A prosperous Roman city in the 2nd–3rd centuries, featuring a forum, a Capitol, temples and thermal baths (winter and summer) which are still visible.
thuburbomajus.a: The Capitol standing on its podium; the paved forum; the winter and summer baths and the Petronii gymnasium.
thuburbomajus.c: A peaceful, undulating site, best visited in combination with the nearby Temple of the Waters of Zaghouan.
thuburbomajus.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

maktharmactaris.d: An ancient city of Numidian origin that later became Roman, featuring Trajan’s Arch, the Great Southern Baths and the ‘House of Venus’. Situated at high altitude in the high steppe.
maktharmactaris.a: Trajan’s Arch, the well-preserved Great Southern Baths, the ‘House of Venus’ and the Schola des Juvenes, set against the backdrop of the high steppe.
maktharmactaris.c: Make sure you bring water and sturdy shoes as the site is extensive and exposed; the visit takes around 2 hours and is particularly pleasant in spring.
maktharmactaris.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

chemtousimitthus.d: An ancient site famous for its quarries of Numidian yellow marble (marmor numidicum) exploited by the Romans, featuring a Roman bridge, theatre and basilica.
chemtousimitthus.a: The Numidian yellow marble quarries; the Roman bridge over the Medjerda; the theatre, the basilica and the excellent marble museum.
chemtousimitthus.c: Don’t miss the modern museum, which explains the quarrying of this famous ancient marble.
chemtousimitthus.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

pontdetrajanchemtou.d: Roman bridge spanning the Medjerda wadi near Simitthus, linked to the quarrying and transport of Chemtou marble.
pontdetrajanchemtou.a: The remains of the Roman bridge spanning the Medjerda wadi, linked to the transport of marble from Chemtou.
pontdetrajanchemtou.c: A brief stop as part of the tour of the Chemtou site; the water level of the wadi is lower and the crossing is easier outside the rainy season.

oudhnauthina.d: A Roman colony south of Tunis, featuring an amphitheatre, a capitol, thermal baths and cisterns. An important villa and mosaics.
oudhnauthina.a: The partially restored amphitheatre; the Capitol and its cisterns; the remains of villas with mosaics.
oudhnauthina.c: Close to Tunis, ideal for a half-day trip combined with Thuburbo Majus.
oudhnauthina.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

haidraammaedara.d: An ancient Roman and later Byzantine city near the Algerian border, featuring a vast Byzantine fortress, arches and Christian basilicas.
haidraammaedara.a: The vast Byzantine fortress with its imposing ramparts, triumphal arches, the Church of Melleus and several Christian basilicas near the Algerian border.
haidraammaedara.c: A sprawling and remote site: bring plenty of water, allow two hours for your visit, and check the access details before setting off.
haidraammaedara.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

gightisgigthis.d: Former Punic trading post and later a Roman city on the Gulf of Bou Ghrara, featuring a forum, capitol, thermal baths and temples.
gightisgigthis.a: Remains of a Punic and later Roman city on the Gulf of Bou Ghrara: paved forum, capitol, thermal baths and temple foundations.
gightisgigthis.c: Site open during the day, with little shade: bring water and a hat, and check the AMVPPC’s opening times on site.
gightisgigthis.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

pupput.d: Roman city on the coast near Hammamet, known for its necropolis and house mosaics.
pupput.a: Remains of a Roman coastal town near Hammamet: necropolis and mosaics in domestic buildings.
pupput.c: A modest, out-of-the-way site in the southern Hammamet hotel zone; a quick visit to combine with the Hammamet medina.
pupput.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary depending on the season, so please check on site.

hadrumetehadrumetumsousseantique.d: An ancient Phoenician settlement that became a major Roman city (Hadrumetum), beneath present-day Sousse. Christian catacombs and rich mosaics.
hadrumetehadrumetumsousseantique.a: Layers of ancient Hadrumetum beneath modern-day Sousse: a Punic and then Roman heritage, which gave rise to the Christian catacombs and the mosaics on display in the museum.
hadrumetehadrumetumsousseantique.c: As the remains are scattered beneath the modern city, the Kasbah Archaeological Museum offers the best overview.

catacombesdesousse.d: An extensive network of early Christian burial galleries dug beneath ancient Hadrumetum, containing thousands of tombs.
catacombesdesousse.a: A vast network of early Christian burial galleries dug beneath ancient Hadrumetum, containing thousands of tombs; only part of it is open to visitors.
catacombesdesousse.c: Check on arrival that the open section is accessible, as access to the catacombs is sometimes restricted.
catacombesdesousse.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

neapolisnabeul.d: An ancient coastal city near present-day Nabeul, known for its garum production workshops and a large house with mosaics.
neapolisnabeul.a: Ancient garum workshops by the sea and a large house with mosaics, bearing witness to the activity of the coastal city of Neapolis.
neapolisnabeul.c: An open-air site near the Nabeul seafront, best visited in conjunction with the town’s archaeological museum.

thuburnica.d: A Roman city in north-western Tunisia, featuring a Roman bridge attributed to the time of Trajan and various other remains.
thuburnica.a: The Roman bridge, thought to date from the time of Trajan, is still standing, along with various scattered remains of the ancient city in the countryside.
thuburnica.c: A small, remote rural site: a car and sturdy footwear are essential; best combined with a visit to nearby Chemtou.

mustimustis.d: A Roman city on the Carthage–Theveste road, featuring temples, the Arch of Gordian III and oil mills. Coordinates of the centre of the site.
mustimustis.a: The temples, the Arch of Gordian III, the macellum and the ancient oil mills lining the Carthage–Theveste road.
mustimustis.c: A roadside site that’s easy to explore in about an hour; can be combined with a visit to El Krib.

siccavenerialekefantique.d: An ancient Numidian and later Roman city situated beneath the present-day town of Le Kef, known for its sanctuary and ancient cisterns.
siccavenerialekefantique.a: Ancient remains visible beneath the modern town, notably the Roman cisterns and traces of the sanctuary of Venus.
siccavenerialekefantique.c: Explore these by strolling through the medina of El Kef, which lies over the ancient city.

cilliumkasserine.d: A Roman city near Kasserine, featuring a theatre, an arch and the Flavii mausoleum. Approximate coordinates of the ancient site.
cilliumkasserine.a: The theatre, the arch and, above all, the three-storey Mausoleum of the Flavii, in the ancient area on the outskirts of Kasserine.
cilliumkasserine.c: Approximate coordinates of the area: first locate the Mausoleum of the Flavii, which is the most visible feature.

batailledezamaemplacementpresume.d: Site of Scipio Africanus’s victory over Hannibal at the end of the Second Punic War. The exact location remains a matter of debate; presumed coordinates (Wikidata), to be regarded as approximate.
batailledezamaemplacementpresume.a: No remains to be seen: this is a site commemorating Scipio’s victory over Hannibal (202 BC), the exact location of which remains a matter of debate.
batailledezamaemplacementpresume.c: A site of purely historical interest; the main attraction lies in the ancient cities in the surrounding area (Zama Regia, Naraggara).

medinadetunis.d: The historic heart of Tunis, founded in the 7th–9th centuries, with a dense network of souks, mosques and palaces. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
medinadetunis.a: The Zitouna Mosque; the covered souks (perfumers, chechias); the Dar Hussein and Dar Lasram palaces; the Bab Bhar and Bab Jedid gates; the panoramic terraces of the cafés.
medinadetunis.c: Lose yourself here in the morning when the souks come to life; head up to a café terrace for views of the minarets.

mosqueezitounagrandemosqueedetunis.d: The Great Mosque and the main religious monument of the Medina of Tunis, founded during the Umayyad/Aghlabid period, and long a centre of learning.
mosqueezitounagrandemosqueedetunis.a: The large prayer hall with its reused ancient columns; the vast paved courtyard and its sundial; the minaret.
mosqueezitounagrandemosqueedetunis.c: Modest dress required; the courtyard is open to non-Muslim visitors during the day.
mosqueezitounagrandemosqueedetunis.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate attire required.

mosqueesidimahreztunis.d: Ottoman-era mosque in the medina of Tunis, notable for its Ottoman-inspired domes, dedicated to the city’s patron saint.
mosqueesidimahreztunis.a: the ensemble of white domes inspired by the Ottoman style of Istanbul, unique to Tunis; the zaouïa of the patron saint opposite.
mosqueesidimahreztunis.c: A striking silhouette visible from the narrow streets of the Bab Souika district.

grandemosqueedekairouan.d: The Great Mosque of Kairouan (Oqba ibn Nafi Mosque), one of the oldest and most important religious complexes in the Muslim West, founded in the 7th century.
grandemosqueedekairouan.a: the vast courtyard and its sundial; the massive three-storey minaret; the prayer hall with its reused columns and mihrab adorned with lustre tiles.
grandemosqueedekairouan.c: Appropriate attire is required; the courtyard is open to visitors, whilst the prayer hall can be viewed from the threshold.
grandemosqueedekairouan.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate attire required.

raqqada.d: Former princely residence and Aghlabid capital south of Kairouan. Site of the National Museum of Islamic Art.
raqqada.a: Former Aghlabid princely capital south of Kairouan, now best known for its National Museum of Islamic Art (Kairouan Qur’anic manuscripts).
raqqada.c: Site some distance from the centre: combine this visit with a trip to Kairouan by car.

almansuriyasabra.d: Former Fatimid and later Zirid palatial city near Kairouan, now largely lost. Approximate coordinates of the site.
almansuriyasabra.a: Heavily levelled remains of a Fatimid and later Zirid palatial city, now largely lost; of mainly archaeological interest.
almansuriyasabra.c: Site poorly developed and difficult to interpret: best suited to archaeology enthusiasts, ideally accompanied by a guide.

medinadesousse.d: The fortified medina of Sousse with its ramparts, kasbah, ribat and grand mosque. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
medinadesousse.a: the crenellated ramparts; the ribat and its watchtower; the kasbah, home to the museum and its mosaics; the Great Mosque.
medinadesousse.c: Climb up to the ribat tower or the kasbah for views of the medina and the harbour.

ribatdesousse.d: The Ribat (fortified monastery) of Sousse, built during the Aghlabid period (8th–9th centuries), with its watchtower (nador) overlooking the medina.
ribatdesousse.a: The fortified courtyard and the cells of the monk-soldiers; the oratory; the watchtower (nador) offering a panoramic view of the medina.
ribatdesousse.c: Climb the narrow tower early in the morning to catch the light and avoid the crowds.
ribatdesousse.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

grandemosqueedesousse.d: The 9th-century Great Mosque of Sousse, with its simple, fortified layout, is situated in the heart of the medina near the ribat.
grandemosqueedesousse.a: the courtyard lined with galleries; the corner turrets reminiscent of a fortress; the simple Aghlabid prayer hall.
grandemosqueedesousse.c: Just a stone’s throw from the ribat, well worth including in the same tour of the medina.
grandemosqueedesousse.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate dress required.

ribatdemonastir.d: The Ribat of Monastir, one of the oldest Islamic defensive structures in Ifriqiya (founded around 796), expanded over the centuries.
ribatdemonastir.a: A labyrinth of courtyards, rooms and staircases; the panoramic watchtower; the Museum of Islamic Art housed within the complex.
ribatdemonastir.c: A setting for famous films; climb the tower for views of the sea and the Bourguiba mausoleum.
ribatdemonastir.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

grandemosqueedemonastir.d: The Great Mosque of Monastir, adjacent to the ribat, dates from the Middle Ages and has been remodelled several times.
grandemosqueedemonastir.a: A mosque of medieval origin that has been remodelled several times, situated right next to the ribat.
grandemosqueedemonastir.c: Best visited in conjunction with the nearby ribat; appropriate attire required.
grandemosqueedemonastir.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate attire required.

mahdiamedinaetsitehistorique.d: Former Fatimid capital founded in the 10th century on a fortified peninsula, featuring its monumental gate (Skifa Kahla) and its grand mosque.
mahdiamedinaetsitehistorique.a: the monumental Skifa Kahla gate; the reconstructed Fatimid Great Mosque; the Borj el-Kebir; the maritime cemetery and Cape Afrique.
mahdiamedinaetsitehistorique.c: Take a stroll around the peninsula at sunset; the fishing harbour comes to life early in the morning.

grandemosqueedemahdia.d: The Great Fatimid Mosque of Mahdia, rebuilt identically in the 20th century based on its original 10th-century plans.
grandemosqueedemahdia.a: the monumental portico façade and its projecting gateway, a reconstruction of the 10th-century Fatimid plan; the courtyard opening out onto the sea.
grandemosqueedemahdia.c: Beautiful late-afternoon light on the light-coloured stone, facing the harbour.
grandemosqueedemahdia.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate dress required.

grandemosqueedesfax.d: The Great Mosque in the heart of the Sfax medina, founded during the Aghlabid period (9th century) and enlarged on several occasions.
grandemosqueedesfax.a: The minaret with its carved geometric decoration; the façades adorned with inscriptions; its location at the heart of the medina’s souks.
grandemosqueedesfax.c: Walk around the minaret through the narrow streets of the souks to take in the decorations.
grandemosqueedesfax.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate attire required.

grandemosqueedetestour.d: Testour Mosque, in a town founded in the 17th century by Andalusians (Moriscos) expelled from Spain; minaret with Hispano-Moorish influences, featuring a clock.
grandemosqueedetestour.a: the Hispano-Moorish minaret with a clock; the Andalusian décor brought by the Moriscos; the town square of the town founded in the 17th century.
grandemosqueedetestour.c: Combine with the Malouf festival in summer; picturesque Andalusian village on the Medjerda.
grandemosqueedetestour.h: Place of worship — visits possible during opening hours; appropriate dress required.

lekefkasbahetmedina.d: A hilltop town in the north-west dominated by its Ottoman kasbah, built on top of the ancient Sicca Veneria. A complex of mosques, zaouias and a basilica.
lekefkasbahetmedina.a: The Ottoman kasbah overlooking the town, the medina with its mosques and zaouias, and the early Christian basilica of Dar El Kous, all built on top of the ancient Sicca Veneria.
lekefkasbahetmedina.c: A hilltop town that is pleasant to explore on foot; allow half a day and make sure you have good shoes for the sloping alleyways.

basiliquesaintpierredarelkouslekef.d: The ancient Christian basilica (known as Dar El Kous) in Le Kef, one of the best-preserved early Christian buildings in Tunisia.
basiliquesaintpierredarelkouslekef.a: One of the best-preserved early Christian buildings in Tunisia, with its apse and arches still intact.
basiliquesaintpierredarelkouslekef.c: A short visit to the heart of El Kef, to be included as part of a tour of the medina.

synagoguedelaghribadjerba.d: The oldest synagogue in Tunisia, in Erriadh (Hara Seghira) on the island of Djerba, a site of annual Jewish pilgrimage.
synagoguedelaghribadjerba.a: The oldest synagogue in Tunisia, in Erriadh, with an interior lined with faience tiles and the site of an annual Jewish pilgrimage.
synagoguedelaghribadjerba.c: Appropriate attire is required; visitor numbers peak during the spring pilgrimage (Lag Ba’omer).

mosqueededjerbaarchitecturedjerbienne.d: A traditional mosque in the Djerban architectural style, with whitewashed walls and domes characteristic of the island.
mosqueededjerbaarchitecturedjerbienne.a: Typical Djerbian architecture: whitewashed walls, rounded domes and clean lines.
mosqueededjerbaarchitecturedjerbienne.c: Access to the interior may be restricted to worshippers; be sure to admire the white walls bathed in low-angled light.

meninx.d: The main ancient city on the island of Djerba, renowned in antiquity for its production of purple dye. Remains of the forum and amphitheatre.
meninx.a: Djerba’s main ancient city, once renowned for its purple dye: remains of the forum and ruins of buildings in the south of the island.
meninx.c: An open-air archaeological site, largely undeveloped: closed-toe shoes and water are recommended.

ksarouledsoltane.d: A Berber ksar with ghorfas (multi-storey storage cells) south of Tataouine, among the best-preserved in southern Tunisia.
ksarouledsoltane.a: One of the best-preserved ksour with ghorfas in the south, its storage cells stacked over several storeys around courtyards.
ksarouledsoltane.c: Lighting and photo opportunities are best at the end of the day; the site is managed by the AMVPPC – opening times should be checked on site.
ksarouledsoltane.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, to be checked on site.

cheniniksaretvillage.d: A hilltop Berber village in the Tataouine region, organised around a ridge-top ksar and fortified granaries.
cheniniksaretvillage.a: A hilltop Berber village centred around a ridge-top ksar and fortified granaries, with its white mosque below.
cheniniksaretvillage.c: Ascent via a rocky path: wear sturdy footwear and visit early in the morning to avoid the heat.

douiretksaretvillage.d: A Berber cave village and its hilltop ksar, south-west of Tataouine, long inhabited by an Amazigh community.
douiretksaretvillage.a: A Berber cave village and its hilltop ksar, long inhabited by an Amazigh community.
douiretksaretvillage.c: Steep, exposed terrain: bring water, a hat and walking shoes.

guermessaksaretvillage.d: A hilltop Berber village with a ksar on the ridge, in the Tataouine region, less crowded than Chenini and Douiret.
guermessaksaretvillage.a: A hilltop Berber village with a hilltop ksar, quieter and less crowded than Chenini and Douiret.
guermessaksaretvillage.c: Access can be tricky at times: a 4x4 or a local guide makes the climb easier.

ksarhadada.d: Ksar a Ghorfas, north of Tataouine (Ghomrassen region), partially restored.
ksarhadada.a: Partially restored Ksar a Ghorfas, north of Tataouine near Ghomrassen.
ksarhadada.c: A quick visit is possible; can be combined with the neighbouring ksours in the Ghomrassen region.

ksarhallouf.d: A fortified ksar in the Medenine region (Beni Khedache), standing on a hill overlooking the valley.
ksarhallouf.a: A fortified ksar stands on a hill overlooking the valley, in the Beni Khedache region.
ksarhallouf.c: Mountain road: drive carefully and take water to cope with the heat.

matmata.d: A Berber village known for its cave dwellings carved into the ground in a crater-like formation. Coordinates of the village centre.
matmata.a: Village known for its cave dwellings carved into the ground in a crater-like formation, arranged around circular courtyards.
matmata.c: Some houses are open to visitors; please respect the residents’ privacy and avoid visiting during the hottest part of the day.

toujane.d: A Berber mountain village clinging to the slopes of the Matmata mountains, renowned for its weaving and terraced landscape.
toujane.a: A Berber village clinging to the slopes of the Matmata mountains, renowned for its weaving and terraced fields.
toujane.c: The scenic route from Matmata is superb: drive slowly to enjoy the views.

takrouna.d: A Berber village perched on a rocky outcrop near Enfidha, with its ancient whitewashed buildings. Approximate coordinates of the village summit.
takrouna.a: The old white village perched on its rocky outcrop; the zaouïa at the summit; the 360° view over the Sahel plain.
takrouna.c: Climb to the top for the panoramic view; there’s a café overlooking the village.

salaktasullecthum.d: Ancient Roman port of the Sahel (Sullecthum), a centre for the production and export of oil and garum. Small museum and coastal ruins.
salaktasullecthum.a: Ancient Roman port of the Sahel, a centre for the production of oil and garum: coastal ruins and a small local museum (lion mosaic).
salaktasullecthum.c: Combine a visit to the site and its museum with a stroll along the seafront.

thaenaethyna.d: A Roman city south of Sfax, at the far end of the Fossa Regia, featuring thermal baths, basilicas and mosaics.
thaenaethyna.a: A Roman city south of Sfax, at the far end of the Fossa Regia: remains of thermal baths, basilicas and mosaics.
thaenaethyna.c: A sprawling site with little shade, right by the sea: make sure you bring water and wear sturdy shoes.

templedeseauxdezaghouan.d: A monumental nymphaeum built at the foot of Djebel Zaghouan, capturing the springs that fed the Carthage aqueduct.
templedeseauxdezaghouan.a: The Roman nymphaeum, shaped like a semicircle and nestled against the side of the djebel, with its basin and niches that collected the springs feeding the Carthage aqueduct, set in wooded surroundings.
templedeseauxdezaghouan.c: Above the town of Zaghouan; a lovely, cool spot to stop off at, to be combined with a hike up to the national park.

limestripolitanusfrontieresaharienne.d: A system of fortifications and tracks controlling the southern border of Roman Africa (outposts, forts, centenaria) in the pre-Saharan region. Approximate coordinates for a sector.
limestripolitanusfrontieresaharienne.a: A network of Roman forts, outposts and tracks controlling the Saharan frontier; scattered remains in the pre-Saharan region.
limestripolitanusfrontieresaharienne.c: Extensive, desert-like area: a 4x4 vehicle, a guide and a supply of water are essential.

tisavarksarrhilane.d: Roman fort (centenarium) of the Limes Tripolitanus, isolated on the edge of the desert near Ksar Ghilane.
tisavarksarrhilane.a: Roman fort (centenarium) on the Limes, isolated on the edge of the desert near Ksar Ghilane.
tisavarksarrhilane.c: Access via a Saharan track: 4x4 and a guide recommended; take water with you.
tisavarksarrhilane.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

grandemosqueedegafsa.d: The Great Mosque of Gafsa in the heart of the oasis, close to the town’s Roman baths. Region of prehistoric Capsian culture.
grandemosqueedegafsa.a: The Great Mosque in the heart of the Gafsa oasis, a stone’s throw from the Roman baths.
grandemosqueedegafsa.c: The interior is often reserved for worshippers; combine your visit with a trip to the nearby medina.

gisementprehistoriquedelmektacapsien.d: The eponymous site and key reference point for Capsian culture (Epipalaeolithic) near Gafsa, featuring snail shell mounds and stone tool production. Coordinates of the site.
gisementprehistoriquedelmektacapsien.a: The eponymous site of the Capsian culture: snail shell mounds and stone tool production from the Epipalaeolithic period.
gisementprehistoriquedelmektacapsien.c: A site of mainly scientific interest, not particularly spectacular: a guide or the Gafsa museum will help you understand it.

piscinesromainesdegafsa.d: Roman pools fed by springs in the heart of the medina of Gafsa, the ancient Capsa. Two central open-air pools, bearing Latin inscriptions.
piscinesromainesdegafsa.a: Two open-air Roman basins fed by springs, with Latin inscriptions, in the heart of the medina.
piscinesromainesdegafsa.c: A short visit, with some shade at times; combine it with the nearby museum and mosque.

hammammelleguethermesromains.d: Ancient Roman thermal baths still in use, on the Mellegue wadi about ten kilometres south-west of Le Kef. Original pools and structures still fed by thermal waters.
hammammelleguethermesromains.a: Roman baths still fed by thermal waters, with ancient pools and structures still in use, on the banks of the Mellegue wadi.
hammammelleguethermesromains.c: Access is via a track about ten km south-west of El Kef: ensure you have a suitable vehicle and check the road conditions.

kasbahdukef.d: The Ottoman fortress of El Kef, built from 1600 onwards for the defence and administration of the city. It overlooks the medina and now hosts cultural events.
kasbahdukef.a: The Ottoman fortress (from 1600) overlooking the medina, with its ramparts and bastions, is now a venue for cultural events.
kasbahdukef.c: Head up there in the late afternoon for panoramic views of the town and the plain; allow about an hour.

zaouiadesidiboumakhlouf.d: A zaouïa housing the tomb of Sidi Bou Makhlouf, patron saint of El Kef, at the foot of the Kasbah ramparts (from the 17th century), with domes and an octagonal minaret. Approximate coordinates.
zaouiadesidiboumakhlouf.a: The mausoleum of El Kef’s patron saint, with its domes and octagonal minaret, at the foot of the Kasbah’s ramparts.
zaouiadesidiboumakhlouf.c: A short visit, to be followed by a climb up to the nearby Kasbah.

synagoguedelaghribadukef.d: Former synagogue in the Jewish quarter of La Hara, known as Ghribet el Kef, of Sephardic rite. Abandoned in 1984, then restored and reopened in 1994.
synagoguedelaghribadukef.a: The former Sephardic synagogue in the Jewish quarter of La Hara, restored and reopened in 1994.
synagoguedelaghribadukef.c: A small building worth seeing whilst strolling through the medina; access is sometimes subject to local authorisation.

museeregionaldesartsettraditionsdukef.d: An ethnographic museum housed in the former zaouïa of Sidi Ben Aissa, a Sufi complex dating from 1784. Opened in 1970, it showcases the way of life of Tunisia’s tribes.
museeregionaldesartsettraditionsdukef.a: The ethnographic collections on the way of life of Tunisia’s tribes, in the former Sufi zaouïa of Sidi Ben Aissa (1784).
museeregionaldesartsettraditionsdukef.c: Allow about 1 hour; a good stop to gain an understanding of the local culture before exploring the region.
museeregionaldesartsettraditionsdukef.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

thignicaaintounga.d: Ancient city in the Medjerda Valley, near Testour and Dougga. Notable remains of a Byzantine fortress, temples, thermal baths and dwellings.
thignicaaintounga.a: The clearly visible Byzantine fortress overlooking the site, as well as the remains of temples, thermal baths and Roman dwellings in the Medjerda Valley.
thignicaaintounga.c: A quick stop on the road from Testour to Dougga; walking shoes are recommended to approach the fortress.

thibaristhibar.d: An ancient Roman city built on the site of a colony of Marius’s veterans, which later became a municipality. Basilica and amphitheatre; a Christian bishopric is attested from 256.
thibaristhibar.a: The remains of the basilica and amphitheatre of the ancient Roman colony, set in a rural landscape.
thibaristhibar.c: A small, modest site: a brief stop is sufficient, to be combined with the other ancient cities in the Medjerda Valley.

uchimaiushenchireddouames.d: A Numidian city that came under Roman control after Jugurtha, and was established as a colony under Severus Alexander. The Arch of Severus Alexander, the Arch of Gordian III, the forum, the thermal baths and the basilica.
uchimaiushenchireddouames.a: The Arch of Alexander Severus and the Arch of Gordian III, the forum, the thermal baths and the basilica of this Numidian-Roman city near Dougga.
uchimaiushenchireddouames.c: The site is off the main roads: arrange for a guide or a suitable vehicle and combine a visit with Dougga.

numlulihenchirelmatria.d: A Roman city covering approximately 18 ha between Beja and Dougga, one of the best-preserved in the north. Forum with a capitol, two thermal baths, an early Christian basilica and cisterns.
numlulihenchirelmatria.a: The forum with a capitol, two sets of thermal baths, an early Christian basilica and cisterns, in one of the best-preserved cities in the north, situated between Béja and Dougga.
numlulihenchirelmatria.c: A quiet, rural site: make sure you have a car and plenty of water, and combine a visit with Dougga as part of the same trip.

agbiaainhedja.d: A Numidian and later Roman city (Municipium Agbiensium) near Dougga. A late Byzantine fort on a hill overlooking the ancient Roman road.
agbiaainhedja.a: The late Byzantine fortified post stands on a hill overlooking the ancient Roman road, alongside the scattered remains of the Numidian-Roman city.
agbiaainhedja.c: A short stop near Dougga; a brief climb, but make sure you wear sturdy shoes.

thunusudasidimeskin.d: A city of Africa Proconsularis in the Medjerda Valley, between Chemtou and Bulla Regia, near Bou Salem. An ancient episcopal see.
thunusudasidimeskin.a: The scattered remains of this ancient city in the Medjerda Valley, a former episcopal see, between Chemtou and Bulla Regia.
thunusudasidimeskin.c: A modest and largely undeveloped site near Bou Salem: a short stop, best combined with the major neighbouring sites.

althiburoselmedeina.d: A Numidian and later Roman city in the delegation of Dahmani (Le Kef), one of the oldest known Numidian settlements. Forum, temples, theatre, arch and mosaic-decorated houses.
althiburoselmedeina.a: The forum, temples, theatre, arch and mosaic-decorated houses of one of the oldest known Numidian settlements.
althiburoselmedeina.c: Near Dahmani; make sure you bring water and allow about 1½ hours to explore this extensive and largely undeveloped site.

assurashenchirzanfour.d: A Roman town in Proconsular Africa, between Siliana and the Sers. Temples, a theatre and Augustan mausoleums; an episcopal see from the mid-3rd century.
assurashenchirzanfour.a: The temples, theatre and Augustan mausoleums of this Roman city, which later became a bishop’s seat.
assurashenchirzanfour.c: A rural site between Siliana and Le Sers, with few signposts: a guide or precise coordinates will help you find it.

chusirakesra.d: An ancient city beneath Kesra, the highest Berber village in Tunisia, near Makthar. The Numidian city of Thusca, a bishop’s seat.
chusirakesra.a: The ancient remains of the Numidian city of Thusca, integrated into Kesra, Tunisia’s highest Berber village, with its terraced stone houses.
chusirakesra.c: The hilltop village is just as worth visiting as the ruins; combine your visit with a trip to neighbouring Makthar and enjoy the panoramic views.

zamaregiajama.d: A Numidian city near Jama, which later became a Roman colony. Its location was confirmed by an inscription in 2002; the site features a temple with numerous sculptures.
zamaregiajama.a: The remains of the Numidian city that became a Roman colony, including a temple with numerous sculptures; its location was confirmed by an inscription in 2002.
zamaregiajama.c: A rural site near Jama, with few facilities: make sure you have precise coordinates to find it.

theleptesitearcheologique.d: A vast site (~100 ha) approximately 5 km north of Feriana (Kasserine). Baths with mosaics, eleven Christian churches and a Byzantine citadel.
theleptesitearcheologique.a: A vast field of ruins (~100 ha) with mosaic-adorned thermal baths, eleven Christian churches and a Byzantine citadel.
theleptesitearcheologique.c: About 5 km north of Feriana; a sprawling, exposed site – take water with you and allow plenty of time for walking.

sufessbiba.d: The Roman city of Byzacene (Colonia Aurelia Sufetana), on the site of present-day Sbiba. A basilica converted into a mosque, a temple, thermal baths and a Byzantine fort built by Justinian.
sufessbiba.a: The basilica converted into a mosque, the temple, the thermal baths and Justinian’s Byzantine fort, on the site of present-day Sbiba.
sufessbiba.c: Ruins scattered throughout the modern town: a short visit to combine with Sbeitla.

sitearcheologiquedethala.d: A rare town that has retained its ancient name, situated at an altitude of around 1,000 metres, associated with Jugurtha. Necropolis, a two-storey mausoleum and Byzantine fortifications.
sitearcheologiquedethala.a: The necropolis, a two-storey mausoleum and Byzantine fortifications, in a rare town that has retained its ancient name and is associated with Jugurtha.
sitearcheologiquedethala.c: At an altitude of around 1,000 metres: make sure you bring warm clothing, as the site is one of the coldest in Tunisia.

mausoleedesflaviicillium.d: A three-storey tower-mausoleum erected around the middle of the 2nd century near Kasserine, bearing the longest surviving epigraphic poem from the Roman world.
mausoleedesflaviicillium.a: A three-storey tower-mausoleum from the mid-2nd century, bearing the longest surviving epigraphic poem from the Roman world.
mausoleedesflaviicillium.c: The most prominent landmark in the ancient district of Cillium; a quick visit worth including in your trip to Kasserine.

kasbahdebeja.d: A citadel overlooking Beja, remodelled from Punic and Byzantine times through to the Ottoman period. A cultural centre since independence.
kasbahdebeja.a: The citadel overlooking Béja, whose ramparts blend Punic, Byzantine and Ottoman features; today a cultural centre offering views over the town.
kasbahdebeja.c: Accessible via a climb from the medina; best combined with a visit to the Great Mosque and the old town of Béja.

grandemosqueedebeja.d: The main mosque of the medina of Beja, founded in 944 on the site of an ancient basilica and restored in 1922.
grandemosqueedebeja.a: The main mosque of the medina of Béja, founded in 944 on the site of an ancient basilica and restored in 1922.
grandemosqueedebeja.c: Appropriate attire required; well worth a visit whilst strolling through the medina of Béja.

pontdemedjezelbab.d: An eight-arched bridge over the Medjerda, completed in 1677 under Mourad II Bey, featuring reused Roman stones. Still in use.
pontdemedjezelbab.a: The Ottoman bridge with eight arches over the Medjerda, completed in 1677 under Mourad II Bey, featuring reused Roman stones; still in use.
pontdemedjezelbab.c: Visible from the riverbanks; a brief stop along the way, to be combined with a visit to the nearby Medjez el-Bab memorial.

fortgenoisdetabarka.d: A 16th-century Genoese fortress overlooking the old port of Tabarka, a remnant of the Lomellini family’s presence. A lighthouse was added in the late 19th century.
fortgenoisdetabarka.a: The Genoese fort perched on its islet connected to the coast; the ramparts and the panoramic view over the bay and the Aiguilles.
fortgenoisdetabarka.c: Head up there in the late afternoon for the view of the famous Aiguilles rocks.

eglisesaintemaximedetabarka.d: A former church converted between 1884 and 1891 from a Roman cistern. Now deconsecrated, it houses a museum; listed in 2016.
eglisesaintemaximedetabarka.a: The former church, converted in the late 19th century from a Roman cistern, now a museum, in the centre of Tabarka.
eglisesaintemaximedetabarka.c: A short visit to include as part of a stroll through the town; best combined with a visit to the nearby Genoese fort.

museenationaldubardo.d: Tunisia’s main museum, housed in a former Beylical palace in the Bardo. It boasts one of the world’s richest collections of Roman mosaics, as well as Punic, early Christian and Islamic artefacts.
museenationaldubardo.a: The world’s finest collection of Roman mosaics (Virgil, Ulysses and the Sirens, Neptune); the Punic galleries and the artefacts from the Mahdia shipwreck.
museenationaldubardo.c: Allow two to three hours; a highlight of any visit to Tunis.
museenationaldubardo.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

darhussein.d: An aristocratic palace in the medina of Tunis, with a porticoed courtyard, stucco and marble. Home to the National Heritage Institute.
darhussein.a: The marble porticoed courtyard, the painted ceilings, the sculpted stucco and the faience of this aristocratic palace, which houses the National Heritage Institute.
darhussein.c: Access is sometimes restricted as it is an institutional site; well worth a visit whilst strolling through the lower medina.

darlasram.d: A vast patrician residence in the medina of Tunis, built by the Lasram family. Headquarters of the Association for the Preservation of the Medina (ASM).
darlasram.a: The grand 18th-century patrician residence with its marble courtyard, ornate salons and driba (vestibule), headquarters of the Association for the Preservation of the Medina.
darlasram.c: A fine example of Tunisian patrician architecture; well worth combining with a visit to the neighbouring palaces in the northern quarter of the medina.

mosqueehammoudapacha.d: Hanafi mosque in the Medina of Tunis (early 17th century), with an Ottoman-style octagonal minaret. It houses the tourbet of the Mouradite family.
mosqueehammoudapacha.a: the Ottoman-inspired octagonal minaret; the marble decoration and the courtyard; the mausoleum of the founding bey.
mosqueehammoudapacha.c: Worth seeing whilst strolling through the Medina of Tunis.

mosqueedelakasbah.d: The Kasbah Mosque in Tunis, founded in the 13th century under the Hafsids, whose minaret served as a model for Tunisian religious architecture.
mosqueedelakasbah.a: The 13th-century Hafsid minaret, a model for Tunisian religious architecture, overlooking Kasbah Square above the medina.
mosqueedelakasbah.c: Best viewed from the outside from the square; best visited in combination with the nearby Dar El Bey.

babsaadoun.d: A monumental gate to the north-west of the Medina of Tunis, rebuilt in the 19th century with a triple arch.
babsaadoun.a: The monumental triple-arched gate, rebuilt in the 19th century, now stands alone on a roundabout to the north-west of the medina.
babsaadoun.c: Best viewed whilst passing by; as there is no interior to visit, plan for a quick stop.

babjedid.d: The sixth gate cut through the medina’s ramparts in 1278, under the Hafsid sultan Abu Zakariya Yahya al-Wathiq. Nicknamed the ‘blacksmiths’ gate’ after the neighbouring souk. A rare medieval gate still in place, with its horseshoe arch.
babjedid.a: The rare medieval Hafsid gate still standing in the south of the medina, with its horseshoe arch opening onto the souks.
babjedid.c: A good entry point on foot into the medina from the south, towards the Zitouna.

babeljazira.d: The southern quarter of the medina, which takes its name from a former gate – the oldest on the southern rampart, opening towards the south and Kairouan – which disappeared during the Protectorate (its role was taken over by Bab Alioua). Today, the name refers to this lively, working-class neighbourhood.
babeljazira.a: On El Jazira Square: the Bab Jazira Mosque (known as the ‘funeral mosque’), and just a stone’s throw away, the Sidi El Béchir Mosque.
babeljazira.c: A lively, working-class neighbourhood; well worth a quick visit to complement a stroll through the lower medina.

babelkhadra.d: A gate to the north of the medina of Tunis, rebuilt in the 19th century; its name evokes the gardens beyond the ramparts.
babelkhadra.a: The gate, rebuilt in the 19th century to the north of the medina, whose name evokes the ancient gardens beyond the ramparts.
babelkhadra.c: A quick stop on the northern edge of the medina.

zaouiadesidikassimeljelizi.d: Zaouïa in the Medina of Tunis with its ceramic (zellij) decoration, tomb of the saint and potter Sidi Kassim El Jelizi. Ceramics Museum.
zaouiadesidikassimeljelizi.a: The polychrome ceramic decoration (zellij) covering the zaouïa, the tomb of the saint and faience maker, and the collections of the National Ceramics Museum housed on the site.
zaouiadesidikassimeljelizi.c: A gem of faience, set slightly apart; ideal for those interested in the decorative arts, a short visit.

mosqueesahebettabaa.d: Religious complex in the north of the medina of Tunis (early 19th century) founded by Youssef Saheb Ettabaa: mosque, madrasa and mausoleum.
mosqueesahebettabaa.a: This early 19th-century complex, comprising a mosque, madrasa and mausoleum, features marble and stucco decoration and is situated in the north of the medina.
mosqueesahebettabaa.c: Best visited in combination with the Saheb Ettabaa Palace and the Halfaouine district.

cathedralesaintvincentdepauldetunis.d: Tunis Catholic Cathedral (late 19th century) on Habib Bourguiba Avenue, in a composite Roman-Byzantine style. Approximate coordinates.
cathedralesaintvincentdepauldetunis.a: The Roman-Byzantine composite façade overlooking Habib Bourguiba Avenue, and the interior of the capital’s main Catholic church, which is still in use.
cathedralesaintvincentdepauldetunis.c: Right in the heart of the modern city centre, well worth a visit at the start or end of a stroll along the avenue.

sidibousaid.d: A village perched above the Gulf of Tunis, famous for its white houses with blue doors. A listed site of Andalusian inspiration, situated near Carthage.
sidibousaid.a: the Café des Nattes at the top of the main street; the blue doors and mashrabiya screens; Baron d’Erlanger’s Ennejma Ezzahra Palace (Museum of Music); the lighthouse and the viewpoint overlooking the gulf; the small marina below.
sidibousaid.c: Come in the late afternoon for the light and the sunset; a pine nut tea at the Café des Délices is a must.

palaisennejmaezzahra.d: A palace built in Sidi Bou Said by Baron Rodolphe d’Erlanger (early 20th century) in the Arab-Andalusian style. It houses the Centre for Arab and Mediterranean Music.
palaisennejmaezzahra.a: Baron d’Erlanger’s Moorish residence and its terraced gardens; the painted drawing rooms; the Centre for Arabic Music’s collection of musical instruments.
palaisennejmaezzahra.c: In Sidi Bou Said: combine your visit with a concert or enjoy the view of the gulf from the gardens.

museenationaldecarthage.d: Archaeological Museum on Byrsa Hill: Punic and Roman collections from the Carthage excavations (stelae, sarcophagi, mosaics).
museenationaldecarthage.a: the sarcophagi of Punic priests and priestesses; the stelae from the Tophet; the mosaics and the model of Roman Carthage; the view from Byrsa.
museenationaldecarthage.c: Best visited at the start of your tour of Carthage to get a sense of the layout of the various sites.
museenationaldecarthage.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

basiliquededamouselkarita.d: A vast early Christian basilica in Carthage, one of the largest in North Africa, with numerous naves and an underground rotunda.
basiliquededamouselkarita.a: The numerous column bases in the multiple naves of one of North Africa’s largest early Christian basilicas, and its underground rotunda.
basiliquededamouselkarita.c: A quiet part of Carthage; wear sturdy shoes for the grassy ground and the rotunda.

quartiermagon.d: A Punic residential quarter of Carthage, excavated by the sea, featuring the remains of dwellings and an open-air site museum. Approximate coordinates.
quartiermagon.a: The remains of Punic dwellings excavated by the sea and the small open-air site museum explaining the urban layout of Carthage.
quartiermagon.c: A short walk along the coast, to be combined with a visit to the nearby Baths of Antoninus.

villasromainesdecarthagecollinedelodeon.d: Residential area of Roman Carthage on the Odeon Hill, featuring the House of the Aviary with its peristyle and mosaics, and an odeon. Approximate coordinates.
villasromainesdecarthagecollinedelodeon.a: The House of the Aviary with its reconstructed peristyle and mosaics still in situ, the panoramic terraces and the remains of the Odeon on the hill.
villasromainesdecarthagecollinedelodeon.c: Beautiful view over Carthage and the sea; to be included in the site’s combined ticket.

palaispresidentieldecarthage.d: Official residence of the President of the Republic of Tunisia, situated on the seafront in Carthage. A 20th-century palatial complex set within enclosed grounds.
palaispresidentieldecarthage.a: The palace and its enclosed grounds can be glimpsed from the outside; as the official residence of the Head of State, the complex is not open to visitors.
palaispresidentieldecarthage.c: Site not open to the public and under surveillance: do not photograph the surroundings; simply a landmark on the coastal road.

fortdelagoulettekarraka.d: The coastal fortress of La Goulette (La Karraka), commanding the entrance to the port of Tunis, built in the 16th century and contested between the Spanish and the Ottomans.
fortdelagoulettekarraka.a: The 16th-century Ottoman and Spanish fortress guarding the entrance to Lake Tunis; the massive bastions.
fortdelagoulettekarraka.c: Worth seeing whilst passing through La Goulette, renowned for its fish restaurants.

lagoulettehalqeloued.d: A port town at the entrance to Lake Tunis, the capital’s historic outer harbour. A fishing district with a cosmopolitan past.
lagoulettehalqeloued.a: The seafront and the harbour, the seafood restaurants on the main avenue and the traces of the cosmopolitan past (Italian and Jewish quarters) of the former outer harbour of Tunis.
lagoulettehalqeloued.c: Ideal for a midday meal of grilled fish; accessible by TGM from Tunis.

palaisdelarosemanouba.d: Former Beylical palace on the Manouba plain, known as the Palais de la Rose. Home to the National Military Museum of Tunisia.
palaisdelarosemanouba.a: The former Beylical summer palace and its reception rooms, which now house the National Military Museum with its collection of weapons, uniforms and equipment.
palaisdelarosemanouba.c: Of particular interest to military history enthusiasts; check opening times before visiting.

zaghouanville.d: A mountain town at the foot of Djebel Zaghouan. A Roman nymphaeum (Temple of the Waters) and an Ottoman medina with ancient fountains.
zaghouanville.a: The Ottoman medina with its ancient fountains, the Roman arch, the silhouette of the Djebel in the background and, overlooking it all, the Temple of the Waters.
zaghouanville.c: A pleasant, cool high-altitude base from which to explore the Temple of the Waters and the Djebel National Park.

hammamlif.d: A seaside and spa resort at the foot of Djebel Boukornine, on the Gulf of Tunis. A former Beylical holiday resort with hot springs.
hammamlif.a: The seafront and the casino – a former Beylical holiday resort at the foot of Boukornine – the thermal springs and the resort’s old-fashioned seaside atmosphere.
hammamlif.c: Starting point for the climb to Boukornine National Park, which overlooks the town.

vieuxportdebizerte.d: The historic port of Bizerte, lined with old houses and connected to the sea by a channel. The heart of the medina, long a base for corsairs and fishing.
vieuxportdebizerte.a: The historic harbour, lined with old houses and connected to the sea by a channel, is the picturesque heart of the medina and a former pirate base.
vieuxportdebizerte.c: A pleasant stroll along the quays in the late afternoon; the starting point for exploring the kasbah and the medina on foot.

kasbahdebizerte.d: A fortress overlooking the entrance to the old port of Bizerte, with its imposing ramparts, protecting the town and its channel.
kasbahdebizerte.a: The fortress with its mighty ramparts guarding the entrance to the old harbour, with its inner alleyways and views over the channel.
kasbahdebizerte.c: Accessible on foot from the old harbour; wear sturdy shoes for the ramparts and narrow alleyways.

fortdespagnebizerte.d: A fort on the heights of Bizerte (16th century), dating from the period of Spanish-Ottoman rivalry in the Mediterranean. It overlooks the town and the harbour.
fortdespagnebizerte.a: The 16th-century fort perched on the heights of Bizerte, overlooking the town and the harbour, a testament to the Spanish-Ottoman rivalry.
fortdespagnebizerte.c: Head up at the end of the day for panoramic views of the town and the sea; accessible by car or a short walk.

borjloutanigharelmelh.d: One of the three Ottoman forts at Ghar el Melh (formerly Porto Farina), built in the 17th century to protect the corsair port.
borjloutanigharelmelh.a: One of the three 17th-century Ottoman forts built to protect the former pirate port of Porto Farina (Ghar el Melh).
borjloutanigharelmelh.c: Well worth exploring as part of a tour of the three bordjs of Ghar el Melh; combine with a visit to the lagoon and its ramli gardens.

borjelwoustanigharelmelh.d: The middle fort of Ghar el Melh, an Ottoman structure defending the former port of Porto Farina on the north coast.
borjelwoustanigharelmelh.a: The central fort of Ghar el Melh, an Ottoman structure defending the former port of Porto Farina on the north coast.
borjelwoustanigharelmelh.c: A quick stop between the other two forts at Ghar el Melh; best combined with a visit to the nearby lagoon.

fortdekelibiaborjelkebir.d: A citadel on a 150-metre promontory overlooking the sea and Kelibia, north-east of Cape Bon. It features Roman and Byzantine elements, but the bulk of the structure dates from a 16th-century reconstruction with Ottoman additions.
fortdekelibiaborjelkebir.a: The fortress overlooking the harbour and the beach; the remodelled Byzantine ramparts; the view across the Cap Bon coast, stretching as far as Sicily on a clear day.
fortdekelibiaborjelkebir.c: An easy climb from the harbour; superb panoramic views at sunset.

kasbahdehammamet.d: A fortress at the south-western corner of Hammamet’s medina, overlooking the sea. A 9th-century ribat used for coastal surveillance, rebuilt in the 15th century under the Hafsids.
kasbahdehammamet.a: The fort overlooking the old town; the panoramic walkway offering views of the white medina and the beach; the flower-filled alleyways below.
kasbahdehammamet.c: Take a walk along the ramparts at sunset for views of the bay.

carrieresromainesdegharelkebirelhaouaria.d: Vast underground quarries some 3 km west of El Haouaria, in operation from the Punic to the Roman periods; the sandstone was transported by sea to Carthage. Approximate coordinates.
carrieresromainesdegharelkebirelhaouaria.a: The vast underground chambers hewn from the sandstone from which the stones for Carthage were quarried; the skylights opening out onto the sea.
carrieresromainesdegharelkebirelhaouaria.c: Best visited in conjunction with the tip of Cap Bon; the galleries offer a pleasant coolness in summer.

museedenabeul.d: Nabeul Archaeological Museum (medina), collections from the Cap Bon sites (Neapolis, Kerkouane): mosaics, stelae and Punic and Roman artefacts.
museedenabeul.a: Archaeological museum showcasing collections from the Cap Bon sites (Neapolis, Kerkouane): mosaics, stelae and Punic and Roman artefacts.
museedenabeul.c: Ideal for preparing for or extending a visit to Kerkouane and Neapolis.
museedenabeul.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

bassinsdesaghlabides.d: Open-air water reservoirs built around 860 to supply Kairouan, among the major hydraulic structures of the medieval Muslim world; a large circular basin approximately 128 m in diameter.
bassinsdesaghlabides.a: The two large 9th-century circular stone basins that supplied Kairouan with water; the viewing platform overlooking them.
bassinsdesaghlabides.c: Climb up to the adjacent terrace to appreciate the geometry of the basins.

mosqueedestroisportes.d: Mosque founded in 866 by Mohammed ibn Khairoun, in the medina of Kairouan. The oldest carved and decorated façade in the Islamic world; Hafsid minaret added around 1440.
mosqueedestroisportes.a: The 9th-century Aghlabid façade adorned with carved Kufic inscriptions, one of the oldest dated mosque façades.
mosqueedestroisportes.c: A small monument in the narrow streets of Kairouan, worth seeing whilst exploring the medina.

zaouiadesidisahbimosqueedubarbier.d: A zawiya housing the mausoleum of Abu Zamaa al-Balaoui, a companion of the Prophet known as Sidi Sahbi, the patron saint of Kairouan. Rebuilt in the 17th century (madrasa, minaret, Hispano-Moorish decorations).
zaouiadesidisahbimosqueedubarbier.a: The courtyards and covered galleries adorned with polychrome faience and chiselled stucco; the mausoleum of a companion of the Prophet.
zaouiadesidisahbimosqueedubarbier.c: One of the finest examples of ceramic decoration in Tunisia; modest dress required.

medinadekairouan.d: The historic heart of Kairouan, a holy city of Islam founded in 670, surrounded by ramparts and home to the Great Mosque and numerous monuments. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988. Approximate coordinates.
medinadekairouan.a: The Great Mosque; the Aghlabid Fountains; the Zaouïa of Sidi Sahbi (Barber’s Mosque); the carpet souks and the Mosque of the Three Gates.
medinadekairouan.c: Buy the combined ticket giving access to the main monuments; this is a holy city, so modest dress is appreciated.

skifakahlababzouila.d: The monumental fortified gate of the medina of Mahdia, a remnant of the Fatimid ramparts erected from 916 onwards. The only land access to the historic peninsula.
skifakahlababzouila.a: The monumental fortified gateway, a remnant of the Fatimid ramparts; the long vaulted passageway leading into the medina of Mahdia.
skifakahlababzouila.c: An ideal starting point for exploring the Mahdia peninsula.

borjelkebirdemahdia.d: A fort at the tip of the Mahdia peninsula, built in the 16th century on older foundations. Panoramic views of Cape Africa and the old Fatimid harbour. Listed since 1912.
borjelkebirdemahdia.a: The square fort overlooking the headland; the terraces opening out onto the sea and the nearby maritime cemetery.
borjelkebirdemahdia.c: Visit at sunset for the view of Cape Africa.

mausoleedebourguibamonastir.d: The mausoleum of Habib Bourguiba, the first president of the Tunisian Republic, designed by Olivier-Clement Cacoub. Two minarets and a gilded dome. Approximate coordinates.
mausoleedebourguibamonastir.a: the mausoleum with its gilded dome and minarets; the marble courtyard and the esplanade; the monumental cemetery.
mausoleedebourguibamonastir.c: Best visited in conjunction with the nearby ribat; please dress respectfully at this place of remembrance.

mosqueebourguibademonastir.d: The Great Hanafi Mosque of Monastir, dedicated to Bourguiba, built in 1963 (architect Taieb Bouzguenda), inspired by the Hammouda Pasha Mosque in Tunis. Approximate coordinates.
mosqueebourguibademonastir.a: The Great Hanafi Mosque, built in 1963 and inspired by the Hammouda Pasha Mosque in Tunis, is located in the medina of Monastir.
mosqueebourguibademonastir.c: Visits are permitted outside prayer times; appropriate attire is required.

ribatdelamta.d: Small Aghlabid ribat at Lamta (Leptis Minor), built in 859. A single-storey square building with rounded corner towers and a courtyard containing an underground cistern.
ribatdelamta.a: Small Aghlabid ribat dating from 859 in Lamta (Leptis Minor): a square, single-storey building with rounded corner towers and a courtyard featuring an underground cistern.
ribatdelamta.c: To be visited in conjunction with the nearby Lamta Archaeological Museum.

museearcheologiquedelamta.d: The museum opened in 1992, situated by the sea at the site of ancient Leptiminus. It houses collections spanning from the arrival of the Phoenicians through to the Roman and early Christian periods.
museearcheologiquedelamta.a: A seaside museum on the site of ancient Leptiminus, tracing the local history from the Phoenicians through to the Roman and early Christian periods.
museearcheologiquedelamta.c: This visit is best combined with a visit to the neighbouring Ribat of Lamta.
museearcheologiquedelamta.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

leptiminusleptisminor.d: Ancient city corresponding to present-day Lamta, founded around 500 BC. Centre of a prosperous Roman olive-growing district: Punic tombs, amphitheatre, thermal baths, aqueducts. Approximate coordinates.
leptiminusleptisminor.a: The remains of the ancient harbour and thermal baths; the small museum displaying local pottery and mosaics.
leptiminusleptisminor.c: A quiet site in Lamta, for archaeology enthusiasts, best visited in conjunction with the nearby ribat.

koubbadesidielmezrimonastir.d: The shrine and koubba of Saint Sidi Mezri (died 1141), within the large seaside cemetery of Sidi El Mezri near the ribat. Approximate coordinates.
koubbadesidielmezrimonastir.a: Shrine and koubba of the saint Sidi Mezri (died in 1141), in the heart of the large seaside cemetery of the same name, near the ribat.
koubbadesidielmezrimonastir.c: Worth seeing whilst strolling between the ribat and Bourguiba’s mausoleum.

kasbahdesoussetourdukhalef.d: Fortress at the highest point of the medina of Sousse, incorporated into the ramparts in the 11th century, encompassing the Khalef Tower (859). Home to the archaeological museum.
kasbahdesoussetourdukhalef.a: A fortress at the highest point of the medina, incorporating the Khalef Tower (859) and housing the archaeological museum, which boasts a rich collection of mosaics.
kasbahdesoussetourdukhalef.c: Combine a visit to the kasbah and its museum; the high point offers a fine view of the medina.

museearcheologiquedeljemmaisondafrica.d: Museum near the amphitheatre at El Jem (Thysdrus), with a significant collection of mosaics. Park featuring Roman villas, including the reconstructed House of Africa.
museearcheologiquedeljemmaisondafrica.a: A rich collection of mosaics near the amphitheatre, with a park featuring Roman villas, including the reconstructed House of Africa.
museearcheologiquedeljemmaisondafrica.c: Combine this with a visit to the nearby amphitheatre to gain an understanding of ancient Thysdrus.
museearcheologiquedeljemmaisondafrica.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

thapsusrasdimassbekalta.d: Former Carthaginian and later Roman port city at a place called Ras Dimass (Bekalta, Monastir). Punic, Roman and medieval remains, threatened by urbanisation and erosion.
thapsusrasdimassbekalta.a: The remains of the Roman harbour and submerged breakwaters; the site of the battle where Caesar defeated the Pompeians in 46 BC.
thapsusrasdimassbekalta.c: Scattered coastal site; of mainly historical interest.

batailledethapsus46avjc.d: Decisive battle in which Julius Caesar defeated the Pompeians led by Metellus Scipio and King Juba I, near Thapsus, bringing an end to the conflict in Africa. Presumed, approximate location.
batailledethapsus46avjc.a: Presumed location of the battle where Caesar defeated the Pompeians and Juba I; there are no specific remains, only the coastal setting of Thapsus.
batailledethapsus46avjc.c: More of a historical landmark than a site to visit; to be visited in conjunction with the ruins of Thapsus.

achollabotria.d: A Punic and later Roman city on the Sahel coast, near Botria. It features some of the oldest Roman-African mosaics in Tunisia (at the Bardo), a forum, two thermal baths and houses.
achollabotria.a: A Punic and later Roman city on the Sahel coast, known for some of the oldest mosaics in Tunisia (now in the Bardo), a forum, two thermal baths and houses.
achollabotria.c: The finest mosaics are in the Bardo Museum; whilst there, do arrange for a guide to help you interpret the ruins.

pheradimaiussidikhalifa.d: A Roman city in Proconsular Africa near Sidi Khalifa, north of Enfidha. Temples, thermal baths, a triumphal arch, a forum and an amphitheatre.
pheradimaiussidikhalifa.a: A well-preserved Roman city near Sidi Khalifa: temples, thermal baths, a triumphal arch, a forum and the remains of an amphitheatre.
pheradimaiussidikhalifa.c: An open-air site off the beaten track; enquire locally about access.

uzitahenchirmakhrba.d: Ancient city and episcopal see of Byzacene (Henchir el-Makrceba, Monastir), near the sebkhas of Sidi El Hani and Sahline. Of Phoenician origin, featuring mosaics.
uzitahenchirmakhrba.a: Ancient city of Phoenician origin and episcopal see of Byzacene, yielding mosaics, near the sebkhas of Sidi El Hani and Sahline.
uzitahenchirmakhrba.c: A modest and little-known archaeological site; of interest mainly to enthusiasts of antiquity.

medinadesfax.d: The historic centre of Sfax, founded by the Aghlabids around 849–851, is one of the few medieval towns in the Maghreb to have preserved its urban layout and ramparts. UNESCO Tentative List.
medinadesfax.a: The medieval ramparts and Bab Diwan; the covered souks, which are still very lively; the Great Mosque; the kasbah and the Heritage Museum.
medinadesfax.c: One of the most authentic medinas, with few tourists; enter via Bab Diwan and follow the craft souks.

babdiwansfax.d: The main gate of the Sfax medina, on the southern face of the ramparts. Until the 20th century, the medina had only two entrances: Bab Diwan and Bab Jebli.
babdiwansfax.a: The main gate of the medina, on the southern side of the ramparts; for a long time one of the city’s only two entrances.
babdiwansfax.c: An ideal starting point for a walking tour of the medina.

babjeblisfax.d: The second historic gate of the Sfax medina, on the northern side of the ramparts.
babjeblisfax.a: The second historic gate of the medina, on the northern side of the ramparts, leading to the food souks.
babjeblisfax.c: The more popular northern side: a good gateway to the hustle and bustle of daily life.

kasbahdesfax.d: Fortress at the south-western corner of the Sfax medina, integrated into the ramparts, commanding the defence of this sector. Approximate coordinates.
kasbahdesfax.a: Fortress at the south-western corner of the medina, incorporated into the ramparts; it now houses a museum.
kasbahdesfax.c: Climb the ramparts for a panoramic view of the medina.

borjelksarsfax.d: Fortification at the north-western corner of the Sfax medina (11th–12th centuries), featuring three towers. Houses a collection of stone carvings.
borjelksarsfax.a: An 11th–12th-century corner fortification with three towers, housing a collection of stone carvings.
borjelksarsfax.c: Best combined with a walk along the medina’s ramparts.

henchirkhachoummuzuca.d: A group of sites in the governorate of Sidi Bouzid, identified as the ancient Muzuca, a Roman civitas and the seat of a bishopric attached to Carthage.
henchirkhachoummuzuca.a: The scattered remains of ancient Muzuca, a Roman civitas and former seat of a bishopric.
henchirkhachoummuzuca.c: A modest, largely undeveloped rural site: of particular interest to archaeology enthusiasts with precise coordinates.

museearcheologiquedegafsa.d: The Gafsa Medina Museum, rich in Capsian stone and bone tools, as well as Roman artefacts and mosaics from ancient Capsa. Approximate coordinates.
museearcheologiquedegafsa.a: Collections of Capsian tools (stone and bone), Roman artefacts and mosaics from ancient Capsa.
museearcheologiquedegafsa.c: A welcome, air-conditioned stop during the hottest part of the day; opening times to be checked on site.
museearcheologiquedegafsa.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); opening times to be checked on site.

lelezardrougetrainhistoriquedemetlaoui.d: Metre-gauge tourist train running through the Selja Gorges between Metlaoui and Redeyef, on the former phosphate mining line. Rolling stock from a former Bey’s train. Station coordinates (approximate).
lelezardrougetrainhistoriquedemetlaoui.a: Metre-gauge tourist train, featuring the Bey’s historic rolling stock, which winds its way through the Selja Gorges.
lelezardrougetrainhistoriquedemetlaoui.c: Book in advance during peak season and bring plenty of water; departs from Metlaoui.

ksarouleddebbab.d: Fortified ksar at Ghorfas near Tataouine, partly cave-dwelling, situated on a hilltop. Designated a national monument in January 2024.
ksarouleddebbab.a: Fortified ksar with ghorfas, partly cave-dwelling, situated on a hill near Tataouine; designated a national monument.
ksarouleddebbab.c: Unobstructed view from the ksar: the late afternoon light is the most beautiful.

ksarjouamaa.d: Stone ksar at Beni Khedache (Medenine), built around 1770. Fortified communal granary listed as a Tunisian monument.
ksarjouamaa.a: Fortified communal granary built of Beni Khedache stone, constructed around 1770.
ksarjouamaa.c: Mountain site: bring water and footwear suitable for the terrain.

ksarbenibarka.d: Fortified ksar with ghorfas in the Tataouine governorate, formerly a communal granary for the region’s tribes.
ksarbenibarka.a: Ksar with ghorfas, a former communal granary for the tribes of the Tataouine region.
ksarbenibarka.c: Short visit; can be combined with the other nearby ksours of the Dahar.

metameurksar.d: A village approximately 7 km north-west of Medenine, founded around the 14th century, renowned for its ksar with vaulted ghorfas on several levels. One of the best-preserved in the south.
metameurksar.a: A village whose ksar, with its vaulted ghorfas on several levels, is one of the best-preserved in the south.
metameurksar.c: 7 km from Medenine, an easy stop; photogenic light at the end of the day.

ghomrassen.d: A town in the south-east, about 26 km from Tataouine, a former Berber settlement in a valley of cliffs and cave granaries.
ghomrassen.a: A former Berber settlement in a valley of cliffs dotted with cave granaries.
ghomrassen.c: A convenient starting point for exploring the surrounding ksour; bring water.

ksarouledmhemed.d: Fortified granary with ghorfas (Tataouine), built around 1855, with ~223 cells on three levels. Restored in 2007 with the INP.
ksarouledmhemed.a: Fortified granary with ghorfas (circa 1855) comprising approximately 223 cells on three levels, restored in collaboration with the INP.
ksarouledmhemed.c: Quick visit; can be combined with the neighbouring ksours of Tataouine.

ksarouledbrahimmedenine.d: Ksar in the centre of Medenine, square in plan, approximately 80 m on each side, with around 140 vaulted ghorfas on two levels. A fine example of the town’s ksar district.
ksarouledbrahimmedenine.a: A square ksar measuring approximately 80 m on each side, with around 140 vaulted ghorfas on two levels, a fine example of Medenine’s ksar district.
ksarouledbrahimmedenine.c: In town: accessible on foot whilst visiting Medenine.

ksarmegabla.d: An oval-shaped ksar on the outskirts of Tataouine, founded around 1400, with numerous ghorfas on two to four levels.
ksarmegabla.a: An oval-shaped ksar on the outskirts of Tataouine, with numerous ghorfas on two to four levels.
ksarmegabla.c: A short stop just outside Tataouine; expect hot weather.

ksartamelest.d: A ksar with ghorfas in the Tataouine governorate, a former fortified granary in the Dahar region.
ksartamelest.a: Former fortified granary with ghorfas in the Dahar region, in the Tataouine governorate.
ksartamelest.c: A modest site; best included as part of a guided tour of the ksours of the Dahar.

ksarezzahra.d: Mountain ksar at the foot of Djebel Abiodh, south-east of Tataouine, with a square old quarter and the more recent Ksar Jedid. Listed as a monument in January 2024.
ksarezzahra.a: A mountain ksar at the foot of Djebel Abiodh, with a square-shaped old quarter and a more recent Ksar Jedid; listed as a monument.
ksarezzahra.c: Access via the mountains to the south-east of Tataouine: drive carefully and take water with you.

borjelkebirborjghazimustaphadjerba.d: The coastal fort at Houmt Souk, the largest and best-preserved on Djerba, was rebuilt in the 16th century. Associated with the corsair Dragut.
borjelkebirborjghazimustaphadjerba.a: The largest coastal fort on Djerba, at Houmt Souk, rebuilt in the 16th century and associated with the corsair Dragut.
borjelkebirborjghazimustaphadjerba.c: Climb the ramparts for the view over the harbour; shade is scarce, so bring a hat.
